Adulation means excessive, over-the-top praise or admiration given to someone — far more than what they actually deserve, or far more intense than what is considered normal or appropriate.

The single most important thing to understand about this word is that little word: excessive. That's the soul of adulation. It's not just praise. It's praise cranked up to the maximum — almost like worship.

Think of a scale of admiration:

Mild appreciation → Genuine praise → Strong admiration → Adulation

Adulation sits at the extreme end. When someone receives adulation, people aren't just saying "well done." They are essentially treating that person like a god or a superstar — showering them with intense, gushing, often uncontrollable admiration.
What Makes It "Adulation" and Not Just "Praise"?

Three things separate adulation from ordinary praise:

1. The intensity is extreme.
Normal praise is calm and measured. Adulation is wild and overflowing. Think of fans screaming, crying, and fainting when a pop star walks on stage. That's not just admiration — that's adulation.

2. It often goes beyond what is deserved.
Adulation frequently implies that the praise is disproportionate — more than the person has actually earned. A new manager who hasn't done much yet, but whose team constantly tells them they're a genius and a visionary — that team is heaping adulation on them.

3. It can sometimes be insincere or self-serving.
Sometimes people offer adulation not because they truly believe it, but to gain favour, to flatter a powerful person, or to get something in return. A politician's inner circle might surround them with adulation — always telling them they're brilliant — just to stay in their good graces. This is why adulation often carries a slightly negative or suspicious tone. It hints at fawning behaviour — the kind where someone almost humiliates themselves by being overly praising.

That said, adulation is not always insincere. A crowd of genuine fans giving a legendary musician a standing ovation and treating them like royalty — that is also adulation, and it's completely heartfelt. The word simply signals that the level of admiration is extreme, whether genuine or not.

Adulation is almost always directed at someone who is famous, powerful, celebrated, or seen as exceptional — celebrities, sports heroes, political leaders, religious figures, military generals, or even a highly respected teacher or mentor. Regular people in ordinary life rarely receive adulation. The word has a grand, public feel to it.

• The young actress was overwhelmed by the adulation of her fans, who followed her everywhere and treated her like a queen.
  • The dictator surrounded himself with officials who offered him nothing but adulation, never daring to criticise him.
  • After winning three Olympic gold medals, the athlete returned home to a country that greeted her with adulation — parades, banners, and tearful crowds.
  • The professor was brilliant, but she was uncomfortable with the adulation her students showered on her — she preferred honest debate over blind praise.
  • The young singer was simply not prepared for the adulation that came with sudden fame.

It's worth knowing that adulation often carries a gentle negative connotation in serious writing. When a writer says someone "received adulation," they are sometimes quietly hinting that:

  • The praise was more than the person deserved.
  • The admirers were perhaps being naive or foolish.
  • The person being praised might be getting dangerously comfortable with such extreme devotion.

This is why you'll often see adulation used in contexts involving powerful leaders who are not being challenged, or celebrities who are losing touch with reality because everyone around them only worships them.

• It is not a simple compliment. ("You did a great job today" is not adulation.)
  • It is not constructive praise. Adulation doesn't critique or balance — it only glorifies.
  • It is not mild admiration. If the feeling is quiet and calm, it's not adulation.

You'll encounter this word family in your reading, so it helps to know them:

  • Adulate (verb) — to adulate someone means to praise them excessively. "The crowd adulated the champion."
  • Adulatory (adjective) — describes something full of excessive praise. "The review was so adulatory it seemed fake."
  • Adulator (noun) — a person who adulates; someone who heaps excessive praise on another. "The king was surrounded by adulators who never told him the truth."
If you ever need to recall this word quickly: adulation = extreme, excessive admiration and praise, often more than is deserved, and sometimes bordering on worship.
